KEY MESSAGE 1...
Morning Update: As of 8 AM, the forecast is on track for 
locations south and east of Albany to see scattered rain showers
as rain showers are making they way in from our south based on
latest surface observations and latest radar scans. See 
previous discussion below for more details on today into 
tonight.

Previous Discussion: For this morning, increasingly diffluent 
flow aloft will lead to an uptick in shower activity along the 
front as it slowly makes its way into western New England. Then,
by tomorrow afternoon, a southern stream shortwave rounding the
base of an upper-level low (ULL) centered over the southern 
Great Lakes will induce sfc cyclogenesis off the east coasts, 
with a wave of low pressure developing along the stalled frontal
boundary. Forcing looks impressive, with CVA, the right 
entrance of the upper jet nearby, and increased low-level 
convergence near the front. The impressive forcing will overlap 
with deep Atlantic moisture (PWATs to 1.5-1.75") ahead of the 
front. With some pockets of elevated instability, a period of 
steady moderate to locally heavy rain is expected across 
portions of southern New England this afternoon. The big 
question is how far west the front stalls, and thus how far west
the precip shield makes it into our region. There will also be 
a very sharp accumulation gradient on the northwestern side of 
the rain shield as well. Currently, southeastern Litchfield 
County near Rte 6 has a 50% chance to see >1" of rain according 
to the latest NBM, but these probabilities drop to <20% 
northwest of Rte 202. Our current deterministic forecast has 
some additional light rain reaching southeastern Dutchess and 
Berkshire Counties, with most of the rest of the region 
remaining mainly dry but cloudy today. Even if rainfall amounts 
end up above the current forecast, the very dry antecedent 
conditions should prevent any flooding concerns. Today will 
again be on the warm side with highs well into the 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain associated with this coastal low comes to 
an end tonight. However, the parent ULL will be slowly drifting
overhead Saturday into Saturday night. Its exact track remains 
somewhat uncertain, but general consensus still seems to be near
or just north of the I-90 corridor. With moisture wrapping back
around the ULL, fairly widespread showers overspread the region
from west to east Saturday, lasting into Saturday night. An 
inverted trough at the sfc extending from the deepening coastal 
low back towards the ULL will result in increased low-level 
convergence, helping to locally enhance coverage and intensity 
of showers. Latest 00z guidance has ticked slightly north with 
this feature keeping it mainly north of I-90. Most areas will 
see at least an additional quarter to half inch of rain, with 
higher amounts of 0.5 to 1 inch possible where the inverted 
trough sets up. Lower rainfall amounts closer to a tenth of an 
inch expected closer to I-84, especially if north trend with the
inverted trough continues. Most areas dry out Sunday morning, 
but some lingering precip will be possible in the high terrain 
north of I-90 as the upper deformation axis passes just north of
our region with some W/NW upslope enhancement also expected. 

As the system pulls away from our region, it cooler and less humid 
air will be advected into our region with W/NW winds becoming breezy 
(gusts 25-35 mph Sunday and Monday). Generally drier conditions are 
then expected for at least the first half of next week, although a 
few moisture-starved upper disturbances embedded in NW flow aloft 
may lead to some light showers for northern/high terrain areas 
Monday and again Tuesday night/early Wednesday. Temperatures 
generally remain near normal (highs in the 40s to 50s and lows in 
the 20s to 30s) across the region for the first half of the week, 
but deeper upper troughing over the eastern part of the country may 
lead to temperatures trending below normal by the end of next week.
